newsitem.title: USA: Republicans urge public to back budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Republicans urge public to back budget amendment.

text.p: In the Republicans' response to President Clinton's weekly radio address Saturday, Arizona congressman Jim Kolbe urged the public to lobby Congress for passage of the balanced budget constitutional amendment.

The president has argued against the proposed change in the U.S. Constitution on the grounds that unless substantively changed it could jeopardize payment of Social Security benefits to retirees in the next century.
"I believe its passage is the true test of our will to balance our budget," Kolbe said in an advance text of his radio remarks.

The balanced budget constitutional amendment would require the federal government to balance its books each year and would make it harder for Congress to borrow money, raise taxes or approve deficit spending.

Kolbe said he believed there was a bipartisan majority to pass the amendment, which must win two-thirds of the House and Senate. If it passes, it must be ratified by 38 of the 50 states before becoming the 28th amendment to the U.S. Constitution.
The battle will center on the Social Security exemption opposed by leaders of the Republican majority.
"Let your Representatives and Senators know you support a straightforward balanced budget amendment," Kolbe urged listeners.
Very close votes are expected in both the House and Senate later this month.

The president, Democrats in the Senate and a group of Republicans in the House have pressed for Social Security funds to be set aside, a move that would force deeper cuts in the rest of the government if Congress and the White House meet their goal to balance the budget.
The Senate is to vote on the proposed change in the U.S. Constitution in late February and the House has tentatively set its vote for Feb. 26.
